hySections.heading: PSY High-Yield Synthesis — High-Yield Pearls
bullets: Mechanisms that are more adaptive, which means those that tend to lead to positive outcomes, effective stress management, and promotion of healthy functioning and coping.
They are considered to be “mature” because they are constructive ways of handling both internal and external challenges.
Less adaptive; can be detrimental with overuse.

hySections.heading: Sublimation
bullets: Redirecting unacceptable drives or impulses into socially acceptable activities.
Example: channeling aggressive impulses into sports, e.g., boxing.

hySections.heading: Altruism
bullets: Deriving gratification from providing money or a service to others.
Examples: donating money; volunteering at a foodbank.

hySections.heading: Humor
bullets: Appreciating the amusing nature of an adverse or anxiety-provoking scenario.
Example: inserting a light joke in a distressful situation.

hySections.heading: Anticipation
bullets: Experiencing emotional reactions in advance; anticipating consequences of possible future events; and considering realistic, alternative responses or solutions.
Example: preparing emotionally when a loved one has a terminal diagnosis.

hySections.heading: Repression
bullets: Unconscious removal of unwanted memories, desires, or thoughts.
Example: a 25-year-old man has no recollection of going to counseling as a teenager when his parents were getting divorced.

hySections.heading: Denial
bullets: Refusing to accept reality or fact, acting as if a painful event, thought, or feeling did not exist.
Example: refusing to believe a medical diagnosis and not seeking treatment.

hySections.heading: Regression
bullets: Reverting to an earlier, more primitive and child-like pattern of behavior.
Example: adult man starts sucking his thumb when confronted with heavy stress.

hySections.heading: Displacement
bullets: Redirecting emotions or feelings toward a substitute target.
Example: adult man loses temper with daughter because of marital stress.

hySections.heading: Acting out
bullets: Expressing unconscious emotional conflicts or feelings via actions rather than words or introspection.
Example: throwing a pillow when upset instead of thinking about or discussing the source of the frustration.

hySections.heading: Rationalization
bullets: Crafting a positive explanation for thoughts and actions that are adverse.
Example: justifying that sneaking into a movie theater is okay because “everyone does it.”

hySections.heading: Intellectualization
bullets: Using complex terminology or detailed explanations to detach oneself from the emotional aspect of a situation.
Someone diagnosed with a serious illness focuses on studying every detail about the disease, avoiding dealing with the emotional aspects.

hySections.heading: Isolation of affect
bullets: Separating feelings from ideas and events.

hySections.heading: Immature

Patients self-medicate with alcohol, which ↓ tremor.

Wilson disease till proven otherwise in younger patients.

topics.title: Neuropathic pain disorders
topics.summary: Presents as pain, paresthesia, and/or numbness in diabetic.

hySections.heading: Diabetic neuropathy
bullets: Presents as pain, paresthesia, and/or numbness in diabetic.
USMLE likes TCAs (i.e., amitriptyline) or gabapentin as first-line for Tx.
Use nortriptyline in elderly if a TCA is given (fewer side-effects).

hySections.heading: Herpetic neuralgia
bullets: Pain, burning, tingling experienced prior to, during, or after herpes or varicella (shingles) episode.
Acyclovir is used to treat the virus; gabapentin used classically for the pain.

hySections.heading: Post-trauma
bullets: Patients who have injuries resulting in nerve trauma can sustain chronic neuropathic pain. Treat with gabapentin or TCAs.
Trauma can result in complex regional pain syndrome, which is neuropathic pain that occurs as sequela of injury that is disproportionate to the injury itself.

hySections.heading: Thalamic pain syndrome
bullets: Damage to the thalamus due to a stroke that results in body pain, usually contralateral to the side of the infarction, occurring many months post-stroke.
The answer on USMLE for severe limb pain many months following a stroke.

topics.title: Seizure terminology
topics.summary: Focal-onset aware seizure (FOAS).

hySections.heading: FOAS
bullets: Focal-onset aware seizure (FOAS).
Formerly known as simple seizures.
No loss of consciousness (LoC).

hySections.heading: FOIAS
bullets: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizure (FOIAS).
Formerly known as complex seizures.
This includes staring into space blankly, as with absence seizures (discussed below).

hySections.heading: Partial
bullets: One part of the brain is affected.
Simple partial = no LoC + only affects one part of brain.
Complex partial = LoC + only affects one part of brain.

hySections.heading: Generalized- onset
bullets: Formerly known as generalized.
Dumb changes in nomenclature. But I don’t know what to tell you.
Involves both cerebral hemispheres.

hySections.heading: Tonic-clonic
bullets: Aka "grand mal" seizure; type of generalized seizure. It is characterized by two phases:
Tonic phase: lasts a few seconds; muscles stiffen and the patient falls to the ground and loses consciousness.
Clonic phase: rhythmic jerking movements of the limbs; usually lasts several minutes.
Following the seizure (i.e., during the postictal phase), the patient may be confused, drowsy, and have no recollection of the seizure.
Tongue biting/lacerations are a HY post-seizure finding. If the Q tells you explicitly that the tongue is normal in this setting, they are telling you it is not a seizure.
Tx for recurrent seizures are agents such as valproic acid, carbamazepine, and phenytoin. I discuss these later in this PDF in the pharm section.

There is a difficult NBME Q where they tell you a patient has twitching of one arm prior to falling to the ground and having a tonic-clonic seizure. The answer on the NBME form is “complex partial,” not generalized tonic-clonic. This type of seizure is called FOIAS with secondary generalization, or complex partial with secondary generalization.
In other words, if a patient has focal neurologic signs preceding a tonic-clonic seizure, this indicates an origin in one location prior to spreading to other areas.

hySections.heading: Status epilepticus
bullets: The updated definition is a seizure lasting >5 minutes, or 2 seizures within 5 minutes.
Definition used to be a seizure lasting >30 minutes, or 2 seizures within 30 minutes.
First-line Tx is a benzo (IV lorazepam is usually 1st -line, but USMLE doesn’t care).
If benzo doesn’t work, phenytoin (or fosphenytoin) is next, followed by barbiturates.
In other words, for USMLE: benzo → phenytoin → barbiturate (e.g., phenobarbital).

hySections.heading: Myoclonic
bullets: A type of generalized seizure that causes muscle jerks lasting less than a second.
A succession of jerks can be seen over a short time period.
The patient will not have loss of consciousness.
Can present similarly to simple partial, despite the EEG showing generalized activity.

hySections.heading: Febrile seizure
bullets: Fever can precipitate idiopathic seizure in 2-4% of children ages 6 months - 5 years.
About a two-fold risk progression to epilepsy compared to general population.
Tx is with benzodiazepine.
Febrile seizures lasting longer than 10 minutes, seizures that are recurrent within 24 hours, or focal neurologic signs more significantly ↑ risk of progression to epilepsy.

hySections.heading: Absence seizure
bullets: Vignette will be a kid staring off into space in class for 30 seconds spacing out, sometimes with rapid blinking.
This is considered loss of consciousness.
EEG shows symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
Tx is ethosuximide (thalamic calcium channel blocker).

topics.title: Epilepsy disorders
topics.summary: Most common epilepsy disorder. Originates at the medial temporal lobe.

hySections.heading: Temporal lobe epilepsy
bullets: Most common epilepsy disorder. Originates at the medial temporal lobe.
Seizures are often precedes by visual auras, or warning signs. These can manifest as gustatory/olfactory sensations or déj→ vu.
FOIAS are most common type, with or without secondary generalization.
For USMLE, pick “medial temporal lobe,” or just “temporal lobe,” if they ask for the origin of a seizure in the absence of any preceding neurologic findings.

hySections.heading: West syndrome
bullets: Aka infantile spasms; X-linked recessive.
Epilepsy syndrome in infants characterized by – you’d never guess it – spasms.
Causes an abnormal EEG pattern called hypsarrhythmia, which is chaotic pattern.
Leads to intellectual disability.
Treatment is with ACTH (obscure, but apparently ↑ endogenous cortisol, which can mitigate the progression).

hySections.heading: Lennox-Gastaut
bullets: Severe childhood-onset epilepsy characterized by near-daily seizures and cognitive decline (hyperoralism is a sign of cognitive regression [babies put things in their mouths]).
Poor prognosis, with 5% mortality rate in childhood; 80-90% persistence of seizures into adulthood.

hySections.heading: JME
bullets: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
Characterized by myoclonic jerks (usually hypnagogic and/or hypnopompic) that progress to tonic-clonic seizures after several months.
Age of onset is usually 10-16, but can also start in adulthood.
Tx is valproic acid.

topics.title: Autoimmune neuropathies
topics.summary: T-cell-mediated attack against oligodendrocytes and myelin-basic protein.

hySections.heading: Multiple sclerosis
bullets: T-cell-mediated attack against oligodendrocytes and myelin-basic protein.
Idiopathic autoimmune disorder classically in white women 20s-30s who live far from the equator.
Relapsing-remitting type is most common, where the patient will have repeated episodes of neurologic disturbances over many years at varying intervals.
Highest yield findings are optic neuritis and INO, as discussed above.

Urge incontinence is exceedingly HY. Some students ask about overflow incontinence due to MS; I’ve never seen this on NBME. Urge incontinence is what shows up all over the NBME forms for MS. I discuss the incontinences in extensive detail in my HY Renal and Repro/Obgyn PDFs.
MRI is gold standard for diagnosis, showing scattered white matter lesions within the CNS (i.e., both brain and spinal cord).
CSF analysis shows IgG oligoclonal bands.
Clonus and (+) Babinski sign (UMN findings) also HY.
Tx is steroids for acute flares (IV methylprednisolone).
b-interferon is what USMLE wants between flares to decrease recurrences.
Baclofen (GABA-B receptor agonist) is used for spasticity.

hySections.heading: Neuromyelitis optica
bullets: Aka Devic disease.
Sounds exactly like MS but they will say CSF oligoclonal bands are negative, and then the answer is just “antibodies against aquaporin-4.”

hySections.heading: ALS
bullets: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
In ALS, the lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN) and anterior horns (LMN) degenerate.

There are two things you will see in all ALS Qs, making the Dx very easy: 1) The vignette will always have combination of UMN and LMN findings. Fasciculations, decreased reflexes, decreased tone, and muscle atrophy are classic

hySections.heading: Autoimmune neuropathies — High-Yield Pearls
bullets: for LMN. Babinski reflex, clonus, increased (brisk) reflexes, increased tone are classic for UMN. Serum CK can be elevated due to increased tone. 2) Must have no sensory findings. If any sensory abnormalities (i.e., paresthesias, numbness, etc.) are present in the vignette, ALS is the wrong answer. USMLE will often give vignette of ALS and then the answer is simply “motor neurons.”

hySections.heading: GBS
bullets: Guillain-Barre syndrome (aka acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy).
T-cell- and antibody-mediated destruction of Schwann cells and myelin of peripheral nerves.
In other words, MS = CNS/oligodendrocytes; GBS = PNS/Schwann cells.
Can be described as “segmental and inflammatory demyelination.”
Presents as ascending paralysis and loss of deep tendon reflexes.
Can affect both upper and lower limbs.
Symptoms can start as tingling in the hands and/or feet.

USMLE can say “weakness of proximal and distal muscles in lower limbs and weakness of distal muscles in upper limbs” → the implication is that the weakness has already ascended in the legs but not yet in the arms.

Textbook cause is Campylobacter jejuni, but in almost all Qs they will not give a patient who has bloody diarrhea after a BBQ. In other words, you can’t use this as a crutch. They will just give you the symptoms alone and you have to know it’s GBS.

hySections.heading: CIDP
bullets: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
Vignette will sound exactly like GBS, but symptoms will be present for months and progress slowly.
GBS, in contrast, develops quickly over days and peaks within weeks.

hySections.heading: CMTD
bullets: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
Obscure peripheral nerve autoimmune disease that is the answer on USMLE if they give you high-arched feet (pes cavus), hammer toes, and foot drop.

hySections.heading: Bell’s palsy
bullets: LMN lesion of CN VII (facial nerve).
Paralysis of ipsilateral facial muscles.
Usually idiopathic/autoimmune following viral infection, shingles (i.e., Ramsay- Hunt syndrome II), or Lyme disease.

If the Q gives you Bell’s palsy and asks for next best step, the answer is do serology for Lyme disease. If this isn’t listed (or the patient doesn’t live in endemic area, such as Africa), choose “no further diagnostic studies indicated.” Nerve conduction studies are wrong (this is on NBME). Bell’s palsy is a clinical diagnosis.
IV steroids, followed by a 10-21-day taper of oral steroids is indicated to minimize the immune response.
Ipsilateral hyperacusis (due to paralysis of stapedius muscle) and/or loss of taste to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue are basically nonexistent in questions.

There is a Q on NBME where they say patient has loss of taste following trauma + neurologic exam shows no abnormalities → answer = olfactory nerve (CN I) palsy, not CN VII, due to cribriform plate fracture (loss of smell means loss of most taste). If the Q wanted CN VII lesion, they would give a concurrent Bell’s palsy presumably, since loss of taste wouldn’t happen in isolation with CN VII palsy.

In contrast to CN VII lesion that is 19 times out of 20 LMN causing Bell’s palsy, you should be aware that 1/20 are UMN, which results in loss of motor function of the contralateral middle and lower face, with the forehead spared.

hySections.heading: PANDAS
bullets: As discussed earlier, Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorder Associated with Streptococci is when Group A Strep pharyngitis, for some unknown magical reason, causes a tic disorder, OCD, or ADHD in the weeks following infection.

hySections.heading: Sydenham chorea
bullets: Autoimmune movement disorder seen as part of rheumatic fever.
Chorea = fast, purposeless, jerky movements.
Vignette will give child who has rheumatic fever and then ask about the cause of the movement disorder, and the answer is just “autoimmune.”
I discuss rheumatic heart disease in detail in the HY Cardio PDF.

topics.title: Myoneural junction disorders
topics.summary: Autoantibodies against post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

hySections.heading: Myasthenia gravis
bullets: Autoantibodies against post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Classic vignette is female office worker in her 40s who has triad of 1) diplopia, 2) dysphagia, and 3) ptosis that worsens throughout the day.
Gets worse with recurrent stimulation of muscle (vignette might say the patient cannot perform upward gaze for 60 seconds).
Tensilon test is administration of edrophonium (short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) → patient experiences significant improvement in symptoms.
Tx = pyridostigmine (longer-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor).
MG can be a paraneoplastic syndrome of thymoma.
10-15% of patients with MG have thymoma.
If MG is diagnosed, a chest x-ray should be performed to look for thymoma. If the x-ray is abnormal, a CT scan is ordered.
Removal of the thymoma in these patients can significantly improve/cure the MG.

hySections.heading: Lambert-Eaton
bullets: Autoantibodies against pre-synaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
Presents as proximal muscle weakness that improves with activity (vignette might say the patient tries to get up from a chair a few times before finally being able to).
Tensilon test does not significantly improve Sx in comparison to MG.
Highest-yield point is that it is a paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer.

topics.title: Vertigo
topics.summary: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

hySections.heading: BPPV
bullets: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Vertigo is the feeling of the room spinning.
Brief episodes of dizziness, usually 30-60 seconds, sometimes with vomiting.
Caused by a semicircular canal otolith (ear stone; aka otoconia).

Otoconia made of calcium carbonate are normally found within the utricle and saccule of the inner ear and play a role in detecting acceleration and motion. If one becomes dislodged and enters the semicircular canals, BPPV results.

Diagnosis is made via Dix-Hallpike maneuver. In this test, nystagmus is induced when the patient is rapidly moved from a seated position to lying down with the head tilted backward and turned to one side. If nystagmus occurs, Dx = BPPV.
Tx is Epley maneuver, which is a series of head movements aimed at moving the semicircular canal otolith back to the utricle, thereby curing the BPPV.

hySections.heading: Vestibular neuritis
bullets: Viral infection + vertigo.
Inflammation of the vestibular nerve (branch of CN VIII, vestibulocochlear nerve).

hySections.heading: Labyrinthitis
bullets: Viral infection + vertigo +/- tinnitus.
Inflammation of both the vestibular nerve and cochlear nerve.

This distinction of “VN is just vertigo whereas labyrinthitis is also tinnitus” is perpetuated on the internet, but I can tell you there is an NBME Q for Step 1 (that is repeated across forms) where they don’t mention anything about tinnitus and the answer is labyrinthitis (where vestibular neuritis isn’t listed). This is why I write “+/-“ for tinnitus above.

hySections.heading: Vertigo — High-Yield Pearls

I’ve seen the NBME write in the stem “abnormal light reflex,” which is a confusing point, since this could be misconstrued as referring to the eyes, not the ear. topics.title: headache types
topics.summary: 11/10 lancinating, knife-like pain that occurs as episodes lasting usually <1 minute.

hySections.heading: Trigeminal neuralgia
bullets: 11/10 lancinating, knife-like pain that occurs as episodes lasting usually <1 minute.
Classically brought on by minor stimuli, such as brushing one’s hair/teeth, or a gust of wind.
Thought to be caused by trigeminal nerve irritation or impingement (i.e., at the exit points from the skull).
There is an NBME Q where they ask what part of the brain is impaired (i.e., they don’t list any nerves), and the answer is pons, since CN V originates from the pons.
Prophylaxis is carbamazepine.
There is no Tx for acute episodes since pain lasts such short duration.
Often confused with cluster headache if occurring in the V1 (ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve) distribution.

hySections.heading: Cluster headache
bullets: Male 20s-40s who wakes up from sleep with 11/10 lancinating, knife-like headache; often associated with ipsilateral lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and sometimes pupillary changes (I’ve seen NBME say ipsilateral miotic pupil).
Episodes last minutes to half hour (longer than trigeminal neuralgia), where the Q will say the guy wakes up from sleep + paces around his room until pain eventually goes away.
Prophylaxis is verapamil.
Tx for acute episodes is oxygen (bizarre, unless patient has O2 tank lying around).

hySections.heading: Migraine
bullets: Unilateral throbbing/pounding headache that lasts hours.
Can be associated with prodromal visual aura or sounds.
Prophylaxis is propranolol.
Tx is NSAIDs first, followed by triptans (e.g., sumatriptan).
Triptans are serotonin (5HT) receptor agonists.
Triptans are not prophylactic meds; they are only used as abortive therapy.
USMLE will give 30s female with hypertension who has migraine Hx, and the treatment is “beta blockade” for her HTN management.
Estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in patients who have migraine with aura.

hySections.heading: Tension headache
bullets: Bilateral, dull, band-like headache.
Treated with sleep and acetaminophen.

hySections.heading: Temporal arteritis
bullets: Aka giant cell arteritis.
9/10 Qs will be painful unilateral headache in patient over 50. I’ve seen one Q on NBME where it’s bilateral.
Flares can be associated with low-grade fever and high ESR.

Patients can get proximal muscle pain and stiffness. This is polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). The two do not always go together, but the association is HY. (Do not confuse PMR with polymyositis. The latter will present with ↑ CK and/or proximal muscle weakness on physical exam. PMR won’t have either of these findings. )
Patients can get pain with chewing. This is jaw claudication (pain with chewing).
Highest yield point is we give steroids before biopsy in order to prevent blindness.
An NBME has “ischemic optic neuropathy” as the answer for what complication we’re trying to prevent by giving steroids in temporal arteritis.
IV methylprednisolone is typically the steroid given, since it’s faster than oral prednisone.

topics.title: Depression meds
topics.summary: Block reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine.

hySections.heading: TCAs
bullets: Block reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine.
Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine, doxepin, etc.
High-yield on USMLE as 1st -line for diabetic neuropathic pain; can also be used for neuropathic pain in general (e.g., from trauma). Gabapentin is otherwise frequently used.
Have nasty anti-cholinergic side-effects (anti-DUMBBELSS; see HY Neuro PDF for discussion of anti-cholinergic vs pro-cholinergic effects if you’re confused).

Three HY anti-cholinergic side-effect vignettes are 1) palpable suprapubic mass in an older male → full bladder as a result of anti- cholinergic med + BPH. 2) Hot, red, dry patient (as a result of anhidrosis). 3) Confusion + dilated pupils (anti-cholinergic delirium + mydriasis).
Coma, convulsions, cardiotoxicity.
Sometimes the Q can just mention prolonged QT interval in patient on an anti-depressant, and the answer is the TCA, since they’re cardiotoxic.
If elderly, use nortriptyline, since ↓ BBB penetration and anti-cholinergic side-effects.
TCAs, such as imipramine, for nocturnal enuresis are wrong on USMLE.

hySections.heading: MAOIs
bullets: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
Phenelzine, tranylcypromine.
Avoided 1st -line overwhelming majority of the time because of ↑ risk of serotonin syndrome. This can be in isolation, but also when commenced too soon following discontinuation of SSRI.
Selegiline is MAO-B inhibitor used for Parkinson disease. Answer on NBME where they ask which Parkinson med caused serotonin syndrome in a patient.

hySections.heading: Mirtazapine
bullets: a2-antagonist; stimulates appetite; used for patients with depression and anorexia.

bullets: USMLE doesn’t care about MOAs for these. They care about side-effects mostly, as per my observation.
Bind to GABA-A receptor; ↑ duration of chloride channel opening, making them more efficacious (and dangerous) than benzos.
Used for general anesthesia.
Used for unremitting status epilepticus if benzos and phenytoin fail.

hySections.heading: Valproic acid
bullets: Blocks sodium channels and ↑ GABA.
Used as an alternative to lithium in Tx of bipolar disorder.
Causes neural tube defects in pregnancy due to interference with folate metabolism.

hySections.heading: Carbamazepine
bullets: Blocks sodium channels.
Generic anti-epileptic.
Can cause aplastic anemia and SIADH.

hySections.heading: Phenytoin
bullets: Can cause fetal hydrantoin syndrome (finger nail hypoplasia + abnormal facies).
Used for status epilepticus if benzo fails.

hySections.heading: Ethosuximide
bullets: Blocks thalamic calcium channels. Only anti-epileptic USMLE might ask MOA.
Used for absence seizures.

hySections.heading: Benzodiazepines
bullets: Diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam, chlordiazepoxide, etc.
Bind to GABA-A receptor, which ↑ frequency of Cl- channel opening, thereby allowing Cl- to flow into the neuron, hyperpolarizing it and inhibiting it (i.e., ↓ firing).
Hypnotic (induces sleep); anxiolytic (reduces anxiety); anti-convulsant.
Given 1st -line for status epilepticus.
Clonazepam used for insomnia/anxiety (shows up on NBME).
Used for stimulant intoxication (i.e., cocaine, amphetamine, PCP).
Used for specific phobia (e.g., fear of flying).
Used for social phobia 2nd -line if patient has asthma, since we don’t give propranolol in this setting (asked on NBME).
Used for alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens / alcoholic hallucinosis).

USMLE wants you to know that alcohol also binds to and activates GABA-A receptor, but at a different location from benzos. There’s an NBME Q where you have to select the illustration of an alcohol molecule and benzo binding to the same receptor, but at different sites.
Can cause respiratory depression.
Treat overdose with flumazenil (antagonist of benzo receptor).

hySections.heading: Non-benzo hypnotics
bullets: Zolpidem, zaleplon.

Can cause addiction similar to benzos.

hySections.heading: Magnesium
bullets: Used for Tx and prevention of eclamptic seizures in pregnancy.
Given to pregnant women giving birth <32 weeks’ gestation for neuroprotection for the fetus.
Used for torsades arrhythmia and digoxin toxicity.

topics.title: Parkinson drugs
topics.summary: Combo frequently used for Tx of Parkinson disease.

hySections.heading: Carbidopa- levodopa
bullets: Combo frequently used for Tx of Parkinson disease.

Levodopa crosses the BBB to be converted to dopamine centrally. However, levodopa is subject to fast metabolism when administered alone. The addition of carbidopa functions as a competitive inhibitor of breakdown enzymes, resulting in increased levodopa availability for passage across the BBB. Do not confuse this mechanism with direct COMT inhibitors (tolcapone, entacapone), which prevent breakdown of L-dopa.

hySections.heading: D2 receptor agonists
bullets: Ropinirole, pramipexole, cabergoline, pergolide, and bromocriptine.
Used for Parkinson disease management.
Bromocriptine classic agent used for prolactinoma (dopamine agonism ↓ prolactin).

Ropinirole + pramipexole classically show up as restless leg syndrome treatment following making sure the patient is iron replete. New literature suggests gabapentin is first-line over D2 agonists now for RLS, but USMLE won’t play trivia. They will give patient with RLS + say, “In addition to ropinirole, what else could be added?” And gabapentin will be the only answer listed that works.

hySections.heading: Amantadine
bullets: Used for Parkinson disease.
Increases presynaptic release of dopamine.

hySections.heading: Selegiline
bullets: Inhibits monoamine oxidase B, which is an enzyme that preferentially breaks down dopamine.
Can cause serotonin syndrome, either alone, or in combo with drugs like St John Wort or SSRIs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Gross motor:
rapidFireQAs.a: Head up at 3 months (can support his/her own head unassisted). Turn over front to back at 4-5 months. Sits up at 6 months. Crawls by 9 months. Stands/walks alongside sofa at 10-11 months. Walks at 12-15 months.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fine Motor:
rapidFireQAs.a: Pincer grasp at 9 months. Stacks 3, 6, 9 blocks at age 1, 2, 3, respectively. Copies circle at 3-4 years. Copies square at 4-5 years. Copies triangle at 5-6 years.

rapidFireQAs.q: Language development:
rapidFireQAs.a: “Mama” and “dada” by 1 year. Recognizes own name by 1 year. 2-word sentences at age 2. 900-word vocabulary at age 3.

rapidFireQAs.q: Social:
rapidFireQAs.a: Social smile at 2-3 months. Stranger anxiety at 6-9 months. Separation anxiety at 9-14 months. Parallel play age 2-3 (kids play side by side); cooperative play age 3-4. Imaginary friends are normal at age 4-6. (USMLE likes this. No, this is not psychosis). Repeated questioning about death is normal age 8-10. Peds bladder/bowel control

rapidFireQAs.q: "Rule of 4s"
rapidFireQAs.a: After a patient is started on an antipsychotic, a general trend is seen in terms of the onset of particular symptoms. The time frame is not strict/rigid; use it as a general trend – i.e., acute dystonia wouldn't just start at 4 months; tardive dyskinesia wouldn't occur as early as 2 weeks.

rapidFireQAs.q: Acute dystonia at 4 hours
rapidFireQAs.a: torticollis, oculogyric crisis, muscle rigidity without fever.

rapidFireQAs.q: Akathisia at 4 days
rapidFireQAs.a: restlessness.

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism at 4 weeks
rapidFireQAs.a: akinesia / bradykinesia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tardive dyskinesia at 4 months
rapidFireQAs.a: abnormal facial movements (notably tongue).

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient on atypical + gets TD; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: stop the atypical and give another atypical. (Just stop the drug and switch to yet another atypical.)

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for NMS is: the ryanodine channel, which allows calcium to move from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, gets stuck open, so ↑ calcium moves into the cytoplasm. The cell then needs to use a lot of ATP to pump the calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This generates heat
rapidFireQAs.a: fever.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + sore throat + new-onset tic; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: PANDAS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorder

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + given IV methylprednisolone for temporal arteritis + develops confusion + visual hallucinations; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “corticosteroid-induced psychotic disorder”; astute student says, “I thought that happens with high doses over longer periods of time.” → response: yeah, but Psych NBME has it occurring after a one-off dose in a patient. Bottom line is: be aware that glucocorticoid psychosis is tested.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82M + confusion + on various meds; Dx? → various answers on NBME are: “discontinuation of anticholinergic medications”; “discontinuation of diphenhydramine” (1st gen H1 blocker); “discontinuation of amitriptyline”; “discontinuation of doxepin”; “discontinuation of desipramine” (all TCAs) → TCAs, 1st generation H1 blockers, and 2nd generation antipsychotics (atypicals) all cause a triad of side-effects:
rapidFireQAs.a: Anti-cholinergic (anti-muscarinic) Anti-alpha-1-adrenergic Anti-H1-histaminergic

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do you mean by anticholinergic effects of meds?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Start with knowing that DUMBBELSS is a mnemonic for cholinergic effects: Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis (pupillary constriction), Bradycardia, Bronchoconstriction, Excitation (neuromuscular), Lacrimation, Salivation, Sweating → so by anti- cholinergic effects, it’s just the opposite of DUMBBELSS: constipation, urinary retention, mydriasis, tachycardia, bronchodilation not seen (M3 agonism can bronchoconstrict, but dilation is sympathetic beta-2-regulated), Flaccidity not seen, xerophthalmia (dry eye), xerostomia (dry mouth), anhidrosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do you mean by anti-alpha-1-adrenergic?”
rapidFireQAs.a: alpha-1 normally constricts peripheral arterioles → anti-alpha-1 effects can precipitate orthostatic hypotension + fainting.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do you mean by anti-H1-histaminergic effects?”
rapidFireQAs.a: sedation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + develops visual hallucinations after starting on over-the-counter cold med provided by his mother; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anticholinergic delirium caused by diphenhydramine or dextromethorphan (anti- tussive opioid).

rapidFireQAs.q: 82M + urinary hesitancy + interrupted stream + taking amitriptyline; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: discontinue amitriptyline.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + started on new psych med + is now hot and dry; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anticholinergic effects of TCA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + family member Dx with breast cancer + says she can’t sleep; Q asks which med to give
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Psych NBME = clonazepam → benzo OK for acute Tx of insomnia; never prescribe chronically.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35M + recently divorced + stressed + insomnia; which med to give: answers are SSRI, antipsychotic, and zolpidem; answer = zolpidem
rapidFireQAs.a: non-benzo zolpidem may be used short-term for insomnia. Take home point is be aware both benzo + non-benzo can be used acutely for insomnia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + 8-week Hx of progressive confusion and memory loss + myoclonus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Creutzfeldt-Jakob syndrome (prion disease).

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + visual hallucinations + bradykinesia + gradual cognitive decline; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lewy body dementia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + pulls his pants down when guests come over to the house + apathy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease) → characterized by apathy, disinhibition, personality change.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + Parkinsonism + axial dystonia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: progressive supranuclear palsy (student had this on the USMLE).

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + wet, wobbly, wacky + Parkinsonism; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) → urinary incontinence, ataxia, cognitive dysfunction; key point to make here is the Parkinsonism. Wiki it yourself, you’ll see.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for incontinence in NPH?
rapidFireQAs.a: “failure to inhibit the voiding reflex.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Area of the brain affected in Huntington?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on shelf = caudate nucleus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + hyperoralism + hyperphagia + docility; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Kluver-Bucy syndrome → bilateral amygdala lesions.

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of Kluver-Bucy syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: most often due to HSV encephalitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + Down syndrome + forgetfulness; which part of brain is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: nucleus basalis of Maynert → high-density of cholinergic neurons (basal forebrain) → affected in Alzheimer (early-onset in Down).

rapidFireQAs.q: Where in the brain is there high amount of norepinephrine production?
rapidFireQAs.a: locus coeruleus (pons).

rapidFireQAs.q: Where in the brain are there high amounts of serotonergic neurons?
rapidFireQAs.a: raphe nucleus (medial reticular formation).

rapidFireQAs.q: Pharm Tx for Alzheimer?
rapidFireQAs.a: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors first (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine); sometimes Q will ask for mechanism, and answer = “cholinergic”; for more advanced disease try NMDA (glutamate) receptor antagonist (memantine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 74M + MMSE 22/30 + avoids eye contact + weight loss + low mood; DX and Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudodementia → Tx = sertraline (SSRI), not donepezil.

rapidFireQAs.q: Main way to differentiate pseudodementia from dementia?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudodementia is depression that presents as cognitive decline; vignette may describe weight loss or gain, avoidance of eye contact, low mood, and/or tearing up during interview; vignette may also mention poor performance on the reverse serial 7s of the MMSE, or the patient is slow drawing a clockface but can rapidly complete it once prompted (apathy); pseudodementia presents as apathy on MMSE; in contrast, patients with true dementia try on the MMSE.

rapidFireQAs.q: Other notable causes of reversible cognitive decline?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, neuro Lyme.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48F + BMI 26 + cholesterol elevated + HR 55 + creatine kinase (CK) elevated; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypothyroidism → check serum TSH; hypothyroid myopathy can cause proximal muscle weakness + elevated serum CK.

rapidFireQAs.q: 81F + cooks own meals since husband passed away + seems depressed + various non-acute neurologic findings; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: assess suicide risk (this answer is basically always correct if it’s listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: 81F + memory decline; next best step after assessing suicide risk?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE).

rapidFireQAs.q: 81F + cooks own meals since husband passed away + seems depressed + various non-acute neurologic findings + MMSE is 25/30 + no suicidal ideation; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum B12 → subacute combined degeneration (SCD) = pattern of neurologic dysfunction seen in B12 deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which three spinal tracts are involved in SCD?
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral corticospinal, spinocerebellar, dorsal columns → just remember that the spinothalamic is not involved.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + started on various medications 8 weeks ago for low ejection fraction heart failure + now has depressed mood; most likely cause?
rapidFireQAs.a: depression caused by beta-blocker.

rapidFireQAs.q: Nocturnal enuresis; when is it pathologic?
rapidFireQAs.a: after age 5.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + nocturnal enuresis; next best step? USMLE / NBME / shelf wants the following order:
rapidFireQAs.a: Behavioral answer first; e.g., spend more time with child; decrease overt stressors as much as possible. If the above not an answer, do star chart (positive reinforcement therapy; i.e., don’t wet the bed and get a star; get 5 stars for extra dessert; 100 and we go to Disneyland). If star chart not listed or already attempted, next answer is enuresis alarm. Medications like imipramine and desmopressin are always wrong; water deprivation after 5pm is also always wrong..

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient wants to commit suicide; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: admit to hospital involuntarily.

rapidFireQAs.q: Acutely suicidal patient + you need to admit him/her; what do you say?
rapidFireQAs.a: “how would you feel about entering hospital?”

rapidFireQAs.q: 33M + robbed at gunpoint two days ago + now is mute and not responding to questions; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: benzo (lorazepam) → catatonia secondary to adverse stimulus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 39F + >6-month Hx of multiple worries (i.e., career, marriage, kids going to college, etc.) + no overt mood or psychotic Sx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) → Dx is >6 months of general worries without lack of specific stressor.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of GAD?
rapidFireQAs.a: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and/or SSRI; second-line pharm agent is buspirone, which is a serotonin receptor agonist; USMLE wants you to know buspirone + its mechanism, but also remember that it’s not first-line for GAD; SSRIs are.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33M + ingested substance + high RR + now has calcium oxalate urolithiasis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ethylene glycol toxicity → causes calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis; high RR is due to respiratory compensation for high-anion gap metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + found on floor in school bathroom + brought into hospital + sluggish + pupils and vitals normal; which drug/substance did he do?
rapidFireQAs.a: butane (inhalant toxicity); this is HY!

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M + cognitive decline over a few months + ataxia; which drug/substance did he do?
rapidFireQAs.a: glue, not alcohol → 14 is too young to get alcohol-induced cerebellar ataxia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M takes a drug + gets nystagmus + bellicosity (wants to fight)
rapidFireQAs.a: PCP.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + sluggish patient + has angiogram performed (for some reason) that shows decreased cerebral blood flow; drug that was taken?
rapidFireQAs.a: cocaine; this question is on USMLE. Cocaine is known to cause vasoconstriction, i.e., placental abruption, coronary vasospasm; apparently that extends to cerebral blood flow on the exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + injected conjunctivae + has paranoia; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: marijuana intoxication; observation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for OCD on shelf?
rapidFireQAs.a: SSRI (i.e., sertraline).

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + hearing voices for 6 weeks + staying up all night for 4 weeks; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: schizoaffective disorder → Dx is >2 weeks of psychotic disorder in the absence of mood disorder.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the important timeframes for schizophrenia vs schizophreniform vs brief psychotic disorder?
rapidFireQAs.a: brief psychotic disorder is < 1 month; schizophreniform is 1-6 months; schizophrenia is >6 months of psychosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: If brain imaging performed in schizophrenic patient, what would be seen?
rapidFireQAs.a: enlargement of the third and lateral ventricles.

rapidFireQAs.q: Major characteristic in psych vignettes that suggests psychotic disorder?
rapidFireQAs.a: auditory hallucinations; in contrast, visual hallucinations are non-specific and seen frequently in drug use (alcohol, amphetamines, marijuana, etc.).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is bipolar I vs II?
rapidFireQAs.a: bipolar I is worse than II; both will have cycling episodes of mania and depression, but bipolar I will often tell you there’s Hx of hospitalization, or losing one’s job, friends, or relationships (socio-occupational dysfunction), or spending lots of money; bipolar II will tell you patient keeps stable job and/or family life and has never been hospitalized.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for bipolar?
rapidFireQAs.a: lithium or valproic acid to start.

rapidFireQAs.q: Adverse effects of lithium and valproic acid?
rapidFireQAs.a: lithium causes Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy (atrialization of right ventricle in fetus); also tremor and thyroid dysfunction; valproic acid notoriously causes neural tube defects.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cyclothymia vs dysthymia?
rapidFireQAs.a: cyclothymia is >2 years of swinging low + elevated moods, but never meets the thresholds for bipolar + never has true depressive episode. Dysthymia is >2 years of low moods not ever meeting thresholds for MDD.

rapidFireQAs.q: When is delusional disorder the answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: one, fixed, non-bizarre delusion + no other mood or psychotic Sx; presentation will often be patient with mistrust + suspects coworkers and neighbors are attempting to undermine her work or are stealing from her. If the vignette says anything about “aliens,” “the heavens,” “the lord,” etc., the delusion is bizarre and the Dx is psychosis (i.e., schizophrenia), not delusional disorder.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + chronic pain in arm since MVA last year + says to physician “I’m realizing I’ll be like this forever.” Question wants most appropriate response; answer = “have you been feeling like just giving up?”
rapidFireQAs.a: must assess suicide risk.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with restless leg syndrome is at increased risk for what disease later in life?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on USMLE = Parkinson disease (if D2 agonist can Tx, then lack of dopamine transmission may be etiology in some patients).

rapidFireQAs.q: 58M + loses consciousness while shaving + tilt-table test shows no abnormalities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME wants “carotid sinus hypersensitivity” as answer. If tilt-table test (+), answer = vasovagal syncope.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + fundoscopy shows hard exudates + cotton wool spots + scattered hemorrhages; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic retinopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Medication that can cause tardive dyskinesia that is not an antipsychotic?
rapidFireQAs.a: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist); can also prolong QT interval and cause hyperprolactinemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Anti-depressant med causing seizures?
rapidFireQAs.a: bupropion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18M + enters emergency department; which blood parameter would indicate recent alcohol intoxication?
rapidFireQAs.a: elevation of serum GGT.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + 3-day Hx of cutting from 12 beers a day down to 4; develops tremulousness; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chlordiazepoxide (delirium tremens); classic vignette is guy has surgery + two days later has tachycardia, tremulousness, and hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + fear of flying; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: specific phobia; Tx with benzo.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + fear of public speaking (glossophobia); Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: social phobia, not specific phobia; Tx = atenolol (propranolol also OK).

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + fear of flying + must fly soon; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lorazepam → specific phobia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Psych NBME form has both vignettes, practically identical, with the same answer choices:
rapidFireQAs.a: 27M + asthma + very anxious about speech he needs to make soon; Tx? → Psych NBME wants lorazepam, not propranolol (because asthma patient). 27M + very anxious about speech he needs to make soon; Tx? → Psych NBME wants propranolol, not lorazepam.

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + no fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (because no fever); Tx with benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist) or diphenhydramine (1st gen H1 blocker, which has strong anti-muscarinic side-effects).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + abnormal eye movements + stiff neck; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis + torticollis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine channel).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic med + bradykinesia; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: drug-induced Parkinsonism; Tx with amantadine or propranolol.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for tardive dyskinesia?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Psych NBME = “increased sensitivity of dopamine receptors.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-month-old boy + 3rd -centile for weight + slanted palpebral fissures + epicanthal folds + single palmar crease + thin upper lip with a “fish mouth” appearance + indistinct nasal philtrum; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Psych NBME = fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), not Down syndrome; everyone says about this question, so what I tell my students is: if Q sounds like Down syndrome but they mention anything about the philtrum (i.e., long, smooth, indistinct, etc.), the answer is FAS, not Down.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + IQ of 60 + small for age + born to female age 41 + no other information given; Q asks: most likely cause of mental retardation?
rapidFireQAs.a: Down syndrome, not FAS; although FAS is most common cause of MR overall, two points: 1) if they want FAS, they’ll mention the philtrum as per above, and 2) most common cause of MR over the age of 40 is Down, not FAS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + prominent jaw + protruding ears + IQ of 65; most likely explanation?
rapidFireQAs.a: “Fragile site on the X chromosome” → Fragile X (CGG TNR disorder).

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + prominent ears + flattened nasal bridge + long philtrum + low IQ; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: FAS, not Fragile X; the Q mentions the philtrum.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4F + wringing of the hands + putting objects in her mouth + less eye contact; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Rett syndrome; only seen in girls; hyperoralism may reflect cognitive regression (babies put everything in their mouths).

rapidFireQAs.q: 5M + talks to imaginary friends; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: age-appropriate behavior.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7F + preoccupation with death + fear of dying + constantly asking parents about dying; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: age- appropriate behavior. Weird, but the NBME will do what it wants.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + headaches + abdo pain + mild weight loss + fatigue + 5/9 SIGECAPS not met + no mention of low mood; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME wants somatization disorder, not MDD; this Q is a little challenging, as mere weight loss/gain + low mood will often be MDD, particularly in elderly; somatization disorder Dx is recurring, multiple, current somatic complaints; Tx = CBT.

rapidFireQAs.q: 59M + wife says he has bizarre behavior at night where he jumps out of bed and runs back and forth across the room punching the air + says he does not recall such behavior but remembers bad dreams; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: REM sleep behavior disorder → incomplete or absent REM muscle atonia; tends to occur in older adult men; if recurrent, may indicate onset of neurodegenerative disorder like Parkinson disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + gets out of bed at night and tries to leave the house; when his mom tries to stop him, he violently tries to pull away from her; once he got out of the house and woke up outside while in the middle of an episode; he has no recollection of the episodes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: sleep terror disorder; tends to occur in pre-adolescent boys.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + used synthetic heroin + diffuse stiffness + drooling; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: MPTP-induced Parkinsonian syndrome → affects substantia nigra; MPTP-containing powder is sometimes sold as “synthetic heroin.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M prisoner + can’t feel his foot + pulses and reflexes normal; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: malingering (secondary gain – i.e., money, drugs, time away from prison; not willing to undergo invasive procedures) → “no treatment indicated.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Serum abnormalities seen in bulimic patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased serum amylase + hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + repeated purging + BMI 17; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anorexia, not bulimia → if BMI low, answer is anorexia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + anorexia; what electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + anorexia + BMI of 14 + reintroduced to foods; what electrolyte must we notably look out for?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + lost in the woods for three weeks + BMI 27 + reintroduced to foods; what electrolyte must we notably look out for?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: Amenorrhea in patient with anorexia; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased GnRH pulsation → decreased LH + FSH; Q wants “↓ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer; in contrast, premature ovarian failure, Turner syndrome, and menopause have “↑ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Anorexia in patient with edema; mechanism for edema?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased serum albumin (yes, this is straight from the Psych NBME, no idea why).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + has repeated thoughts of harming his son + finds the thoughts absolutely outrageous and disturbing + says he would never do such a thing; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) → obsessions are the thoughts; compulsions are the actions; OCD can be just obsessions without actions; Tx is CBT and/or SSRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33M + witnessed construction accident at work where many people were injured + found by police in bowling alley parking lot talking to himself + unable to respond to questions about his identity; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: dissociative fugue (dissociative disorder); fugue = amnesia for personal identity + travel.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of panic attack vs panic disorder?
rapidFireQAs.a: benzo on USMLE. For panic disorder, Tx = SSRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fainting in panic disorder; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: “decreased cerebral perfusion,” or “cerebral hypoperfusion”; hyperventilation → decreased CO2 → causes decreased cerebral blood flow.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + depressed mood + sleep apnea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mood disorder due to a general medical condition.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + hyperphagia + hypersomnolence + improved mood with pleasurable events; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: atypical depression; Tx = SSRI, not MAOi; MAOi (e.g., phenelzine) are considered highly efficacious but carry dangerous side-effects, so SSRIs remain first-line.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + schizophrenia + poor adherence to medications; best med to give to Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: haloperidol decanoate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F in Australia picking peaches + pinpoint pupils; Q is “how could this have been prevented?”
rapidFireQAs.a: “wearing gloves,” not “use of facemask.” Apparently organophosphate poisoning is acquired through skin, not droplets.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for organophosphate poisoning?
rapidFireQAs.a: atropine before pralidoxime. Retired NBME 15 or 16 for Step 1 has both as answers, and atropine is correct.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57M + trouble with intercourse with his wife + has nocturnal erections; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: secondary erectile dysfunction (psychological) → if nocturnal tumescence is intact, he’s physiologically fine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57M + recently divorced + now sleeping with new women + cannot ejaculate during sex + achieves erection during sex with no problem; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: performance anxiety.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for premature ejaculation?
rapidFireQAs.a: SSRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + comes in dressed all in yellow + high energy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: histrionic personality disorder.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + sexual toward doctor + high energy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: histrionic personality disorder

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + slice marks on wrists and thighs + Hx of two prior broken engagements; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: borderline personality disorder; parasuicidal behavior common (suicidal gestures, but not true attempts at suicide); Tx = dialectal behavioral therapy (DBT).

rapidFireQAs.q: Defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder?
rapidFireQAs.a: splitting: “all doctors are bad; all nurses are good.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + works at plastics factory + quiet/loner; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: schizoid personality disorder (ego-syntonic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 47F + highly sensitive to rejection + poor self-esteem; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: avoidant personality disorder (ego- dystonic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + “wild thinking” + no auditory hallucinations; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: schizotypal personality disorder.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + causes frequent disruption at school and at home; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ADHD; Tx = methylphenidate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + disruptive in class + numerous suspensions from school + caught stealing at the mall; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: conduct disorder → pattern of law-breaking + must be under age 18; in contrast, a patient with oppositional defiant disorder does not break the law.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27M + cheated on the Bar Exam + fired from job at 23 for stealing + arrested for drunk driving in high school; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: antisocial personality disorder; key detail is: must break the law; must be older than age 18 and must have had conduct disorder prior to age 15 → in other words, just because an adult breaks the law does not mean he or she has ASPD. Another important point is that “anti-social” means “law-breaking,” not “not social.” Students tend to erroneously define anti-social as avoidant.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60M + recovering from a recent MI; he is at high risk of which of the following?
rapidFireQAs.a: MDD → common following major adverse events (e.g., trauma, serious Dx); give sertraline for post-MI MDD.

rapidFireQAs.q: Is abuse reportable?
rapidFireQAs.a: child + elderly abuse: yes. Domestic abuse: no. Answer for latter is to provide supportive care + as much information as possible about what she can do if she feels unsafe.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + wife passed away 5 months ago + sometimes hears her voice at night; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal bereavement.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + wife passed away 7 months ago + still grieves; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pathological grief (normal grief is <6 months).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + wife passed away 3 months ago + 5kg weight loss + cries + guilt; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: MDD (weight loss/gain is huge indicator MDD in elderly).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + 1mm pupils + RR of 8 + stuporous; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = Opioid/heroin overdose; Tx = naloxone.

rapidFireQAs.q: Different between obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)?
rapidFireQAs.a: OCD is ego-dystonic (patient doesn’t want/like the thoughts/actions); OCPD is ego-syntonic (patient is content / not looking to modify behavior).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for diabetic neuropathic pain?
rapidFireQAs.a: TCA (i.e., amitriptyline). Second-line is gabapentin

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for herpetic / post-herpetic neuralgia (i.e., from shingles)?
rapidFireQAs.a: gabapentin

rapidFireQAs.q: 82M diabetic + neuropathic pain + already taking carbamazepine + gabapentin to no avail; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: switch the meds to nortriptyline (a TCA) → student then asks, “Wait, I thought you said TCAs are first-line. Why does this Q have the guy on those two meds then?” → two points: 1) we don’t like giving TCAs to elderly because of their anticholinergic and anti-alpha-1 side-effects, so this vignette happen to try other agents first, but if you’re asked first-line, always choose TCA; and 2) if we do give a TCA to an elderly patient, we choose nortriptyline because it carries fewer adverse effects.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to differentiate cluster headache from trigeminal neuralgia?
rapidFireQAs.a: cluster will be a male 20s-40s with 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye waking him up at night (he may pace around the room until it goes away); details such as lacrimation and rhinorrhea are too easy and will likely not show up on the shelf. In contrast, trigeminal neuralgia will be 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye (or along the cheek / jaw if V2 or V3 branches affected; it’s when V1 is affected that this diagnoses are more readily confused) → TN is brought on by a minor stimulus such as brushing one’s hair or teeth, or a gust of wind.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for cluster headache?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = 100% oxygen; prophylaxis = verapamil.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for trigeminal neuralgia?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = goes away on its own because it lasts only seconds; prophylaxis = carbamazepine.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for migraine?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = NSAID, followed by triptan (triptans are NOT prophylaxis; they are for abortive therapy only after NSAIDs); prophylaxis = propranolol.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + diffuse headache relieved by acetaminophen + sleep; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tension-type headache.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + diplopia + dysphagia + eyelid ptosis; all worsen throughout the day; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: myasthenia gravis (MG).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + proximal muscle weakness + able to perform upward gaze without a problem for 60 seconds; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lambert-Eaton (LE) syndrome (if cannot perform, answer = MG).

rapidFireQAs.q: Vignette where Dx is either MG or LE but it’s not listed; answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: “neuromuscular junction.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + difficulty getting up from chair but is able to after several attempts; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: LE.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of MG vs LE?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG = antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; LE = antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

rapidFireQAs.q: MG can sometimes be paraneoplastic syndromes of which cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG from thymoma (do chest imaging to check for thymoma after Dx of MG; if thymoma present + removed, this cures the MG). Up to 80% of patients with thymoma + MG have anti-MUSK Abs (muscle-specific kinase).

rapidFireQAs.q: LE can sometimes be a paraneoplastic syndrome of which cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell lung cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx MG vs LE?
rapidFireQAs.a: If both are listed, choose antibodies over Tensilon (edrophonium) test.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is edrophonium
rapidFireQAs.a: short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do MG vs LE perform with edrophonium?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG improves drastically; LE less change.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of MG?
rapidFireQAs.a: give an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (i.e., pyridostigmine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + ECG shows miscellaneous arrhythmia + seizure-like episode; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Adam-Stokes attack → not true seizure disorder as per EEG; arrythmia leads to hypoxia of brainstem → seizure-like fits ensue.

rapidFireQAs.q: 75M + episodes of loss of consciousness (LoC) for 2 years + tonic-clonic-like episodes + becomes pale and sweaty + Hx of MI; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “syncope” on the NBME (convulsive syncope).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of narcolepsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of orexin (hypocretin).

rapidFireQAs.q: Diagnosis of narcolepsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: polysomnography.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cataplexy?
rapidFireQAs.a: loss of muscle tone usually in response to emotional stimulus (e.g., laughter) → seen in narcolepsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Polysomnography findings in narcolepsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: REM latency: ↓; sleep latency: ↓.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is simple vs complex seizure?
rapidFireQAs.a: simple = no LoC; complex = LoC; patient staring off into space not aware of surroundings = LoC.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is partial vs generalized seizure?
rapidFireQAs.a: partial = affecting one part of the brain; generalized = involves the wholes of both cerebral hemispheres.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of serotonin syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between serotonin syndrome and carcinoid syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: serotonin syndrome is from drug-drug interactions and notably causes hyperpyrexia (high fever), tachycardia, and tachypnea; carcinoid syndrome is a result of carcinoid tumors (usually small bowel, appendiceal, or bronchial) secreting serotonin and causes flushing, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bronchoconstriction.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx + Tx carcinoid syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx with urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindole acetic acid); Tx with octreotide, among other agents.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient witnesses terror attack + has felt emotionally numb for two years since + sometimes disturbed sleep; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “provide information about the ranges of reactions to trauma.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 64M + Parkinson disease + 2-month Hx of paranoid behavior; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is Parkinson disease psychosis (PDP); Tx on shelf = quetiapine (can Tx with quetiapine or clonidine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + survived plane crash two weeks ago + wakes up screaming in middle of night reliving the event; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute stress disorder, not post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); acute stress disorder is < 1 month; PTSD is > 1 month. Treatment for both is CBT.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for TCA toxicity?
rapidFireQAs.a: sodium bicarb → causes dissociation of drug from myocardial sodium channels.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + schizophrenic non-responsive to many meds + started on new drug + mouth ulcers; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: agranulocytosis secondary to clozapine; stop drug immediately; must do granulocyte checks frequently when first commencing this agent.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + BMI 31 + snores loudly + morning headaches + 3-5 beats of jerk nystagmus with lateral gaze; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “sleep-related hypoventilation”; nystagmus is weird finding, but it’s on the Psych NBME; morning headaches are common in sleep-related hypoventilation; can do polysomnography to diagnose. HY PSYCH

rapidFireQAs.q: High calcium + confusion
rapidFireQAs.a: delirium caused by high calcium

rapidFireQAs.q: Bulimia nervosa or anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: never give buproprion (seizure risk)

rapidFireQAs.q: Electrolyte abnormality in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemia

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of death in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: arrhythmia from hypokalemia

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of anorexia + depression
rapidFireQAs.a: mirtazapine (alpha-2 antagonist); stimulates appetite

rapidFireQAs.q: Amenorrhea in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: low FSH + low estrogen (hypogonadotropic)

rapidFireQAs.q: Trichotillomania (eating one’s hair) + GI symptoms
rapidFireQAs.a: gastric bezoar (hair ball)

rapidFireQAs.q: HY drugs that cause agranulocytosis
rapidFireQAs.a: clozapine, ganciclovir, propylthiouracil, methimazole, methotrexate, ticlopidine

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between meningitis and encephalitis
rapidFireQAs.a: meningitis is nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) + photophobia + ophthalmoplegia; encephalitis presents with confusion

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt has tachy + diaphoresis + diarrhea after drug
rapidFireQAs.a: serotonin syndrome (tramadol; MOA too soon after stopping SSRI)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of serotonin syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: remove offending agents + administer cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist)

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M has surgery + two days later in hospital he has restlessness + tremulousness + tachycardia + diaphoresis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal)

rapidFireQAs.q: When is buspirone the answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: second-line Tx for generalized anxiety disorder (first-line is SSRI).

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid is given over-the-counter med by his mom for a cold + gets mental status changes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anticholinergic delirium caused by first-generation antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + last menstrual period 8 weeks ago + USS shows no obvious fetus or gestational sac + curettage shows trophoblastic proliferation; what will chromosomal analysis of this tissue show?
rapidFireQAs.a: 46XX; Dx = complete mole; empty egg fertilized by one sperm that then duplicates (i.e., genetic material is only of paternal origin); complete mole has no fetal parts; partial mole carries 67 chromosomal karyotype → one egg fertilized by two sperm; fetal parts present on USS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + recent surgery in hospital + tachycardia + fever + high BP; what drug should be administered?
rapidFireQAs.a: chlordiazepoxide; Dx is delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal); Tx is benzo (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide). If the Q asks why tremulousness (tremor) present in delirium tremens, the answer is beta-2 agonism.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + one-year Hx of amenorrhea + had dilation & curettage performed to remove miscarriage last year; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: Asherman syndrome; uterine synechiae (scarring) due to instrumentation within the uterus; NBME likes amenorrhea as the major symptom.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born with small right ventricle; risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: lithium during pregnancy is risk factor for Ebstein anomaly (atrialization of right ventricle).
